Legislation Name: SAFE Orbit Act
Current Status: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders
Substantive Effect:
1. This bill authorizes the Traffic Coordination System for Space, which the Office of Space Commerce is developing to provide space situational awareness data and services to space operators. The bill elevates the Office of Space Commerce to a standalone bureau within the Department of Commerce. 
 2. It directs the OSC to obtain data deemed necessary to avoid space collisions, such as location tracking data, positional and orbit determination information, conjunction data messages, and more, and to publish this information at no charge both through the space situational awareness information and services public database and through the basic situational awareness services to satellite operators provision. 
3. It provides immunity for the United States government from any suit arising from the provision or receipt of space situational awareness services or information.
How Does it or How Doesn't it Align?: The report Space Safety and Sustainability, Part II: Policy Recommendations states that Congress should implement bills like this one because its provision of statutory authority for the Traffic Coordination System for Space would strengthen safety, orbital lifetime prolongation, and disposal requirements. It aligns with Pillar 1 in particular because it calls for the Traffic Coordination System for Space to share its data and serve as a backbone for the commercial ecosystem. Does not address Pillar 2 or Pillar 3.
Sponsors/Original POCs: Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX), Sen. Gary Peters (D-MI), Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-TN), Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-MO), Sen. Mark Kelly (D-AZ), Sen. Roger Wicker (R-MS), Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-NM), and Sen. John Hickenlooper (D-CO)

Legislation Name: ORBITS Act
Current Status: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders
Substantive Effect:
1. This bill requires specified agencies to support research and develop guidance on the remediation of orbital debris.
2. The Department of Commerce must maintain a list of orbital debris to remediate to improve space safety and sustainability. NASA must establish a demonstration project to make competitive awards for research and development leading to the remediation of listed debris. NASA must select and partner with an entity to carry out a demonstration mission using technology capable of on-orbit remediation. After the first mission, NASA must make recommendations to Congress to improve debris remediation.
3. NASA and other relevant agencies would be permitted to contract for orbital debris remediation services.
4. The National Space Council and specified agencies must coordinate to update the existing U.S. Government Orbital Debris Mitigation Standard Practices, considering planned space systems and addressing factors including collision risk and post-mission space system disposal. The updated standard practices will inform future federal regulations of orbital debris and international discussions about nongovernment space activities.
5. Commerce must coordinate with specified federal entities to facilitate the development of standard practices for coordinating space traffic and promote their adoption and use for domestic and international space missions.
How Does it or How Doesn't it Align?: The report Space Safety and Sustainability, Part II: Policy Recommendations states that Congress should implement bills like this one because of the authorities it would implement and fund to support debris remediation demonstrations. It aligns with pillar 2 in particular because it tracks space debris and calls for its remediation. Aligns with pillar 3 in that it pushes for the adoption of US practices for international space missions. Does not address pillar 1.
Sponsors/Original POCs: Sen. John Hickenlooper (D-CO), Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-WA), Sen. Cynthia Lummis (R-WY), and Sen. Roger Wicker (R-MS)

The bill proposes no plan to remediate space debris or to create a traffic coordination system to help control the increase in commercial space flight.

Legislation Name: Commercial Space Act of 2023
Substantive Effect:
Would enhance the existing outer space authorization and supervision framework of the Federal Government to increase transparency and efficiency, reduce the administrative burden for nongovernmental U.S. entities  seeking to conduct space activities, and ensure that the United States remains the world leader in commercial space activities.

No later than one year after the enactment of this Act, the Secretary will begin issuing certifications for the operation of a space object to any United States entity that submits an application, satisfying the requirements. 

Beginning on the date that is one year after the enactment of this Act, a United States entity may not operate a space object unless the entity holds a certification issued under this chapter for the operation of such space object, holds a valid covered license, and the entity is from the United States.

The Secretary will require only one certification for a United States entity to conduct multiple operations carried out using a single space object, operate multiple space objects that carry out substantially similar operations, or use multiple space objects to carry out a single space operation.

To be eligible, a United States entity must submit an application to the Secretary, and each application must include a space debris mitigation plan for the space object.
How Does it or How Doesn't it Align?: Facilitates authorization for private sector, does not provide any framework for how to practice space sustainability during this time of increased commercial space activity.
Sponsors/Original POCs: Rep. Brian Babin [R-TX-36], Rep. Frank Lucas [R-OK-3], Rep. Bill Posey [R-FL-8], Rep. Mike Garcia [R-CA-27], Rep. Jay Obernolte [R-CA-23], Rep. Claudia Tenney [R-NY-24], Rep. Daniel Webster [R-FL-11], Rep. Scott Franklin [R-FL-18], Rep. Vince Fong [R-CA-20]

Legislation Name: To require a study of the risk of space debris impacting a metropolitan area, and for other purposes.
Substantive Effect:
The Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Administrator of the Federal Emergency Management Agency, the Administrator of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, and the Secretary of Defense, will conduct a study to examine the risk of space debris impacting a metropolitan area within the next 25 years.

The study will address the probability of a space-based, manmade object impacting a populated area exceeding 1 million inhabitants in the next 25 years, our ability to predict such an incident, our ability to warn the affected area depending on the amount of time needed to do so, the possibility of an evacuation process and how such a process would happen, how federal relief could be provided, including which agencies would be tasked with response, and options to defend against an imminent impact. 

No later than 28 months after the enactment of this Act, the Secretary of Commerce will submit a report containing the results of the study to the House of Representatives Committees on Science, Space, and Technology; Homeland Security; Armed Services; and Energy and Commerce; and the Senate Committees on Commerce, Science, and Transportation; Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs; and Armed Services.
How Does it or How Doesn't it Align?: Analyzes the risk of space debris impacting a city within the next 25 years - does not explore ways to minimize this risk.
Sponsors/Original POCs: Rep. George Santos [R-NY-3]

Legislation Name: National Space Traffic Management Policy
Issue: Orbital Debris; Space Traffic Management; Space Situational Awareness

Sponsors/Original POCs: Scott Pace (Deputy Assistant to the President & Executive Secretary of the National Space Council)

Legislation Name: Strengthening National Resilience thorugh Responsible Use of Positioning, Navigation, and Timing Services
Substantive Effect: To strengthen national resilience, the Federal Government must foster the responsible use of PNT services by critical infrastructure owners and operators. It is the policy of the United States to ensure that disruption or manipulation of PNT services does not undermine the reliable and efficient functioning of its critical infrastructure. Within 1 year of the date of this order, the Secretary of Commerce, in coordination with the heads of SSAs and in consultation, as appropriate, with the private sector, shall develop and make available, to at least the appropriate agencies and private sector users, PNT profiles which will enable the public and private sectors to identify systems, networks, and assets dependent on PNT services; identify appropriate PNT services; detect the disruption and manipulation of PNT services; and manage the associated risks to the systems, networks, and assets dependent on PNT services. Once made available, the PNT profiles shall be reviewed every 2 years and, as necessary, updated.

This aligns because the report recommends turning industry best practices into standardized requirements. It also loosely aligns with pillar 2, as the order calls for a national R&D plan for robust, secure PNT services not dependent on GNSS. Does not address pillar 3.

The Secretary of War and the Administrator of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) shall operate Federal launch and reentry ranges and facilities in a transparent manner that accommodates government and non government users.

It also has the Secretary of Defense pursue on-orbit servicing and in-space logistics to help grow that industry, as recommended by the report. It aligns with Pillar 3 as well because it calls for policies meant to promote US space transportation capabilities and standards abroad.

Aligns with Pillar 3 because it directs agencies to pursue common international data standards and to encourage other nations to adopt US regulatory approaches and commercial practices.

Legislation Name: Licensing Aerospace Units to New Commercial Heights (LAUNCH) Act
Current Status: Referred to Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
Substantive Effect:
This bill makes changes to, and requires certain evaluations of, regulatory processes for licensing commercial space launch and reentry activities and private remote sensing systems.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Office of Commercial Space Transportation regulates the launch and reentry of commercial spacecraft. In 2020, the FAA consolidated launch and reentry licensing requirements for all types of space vehicles into a single set of regulations, known as Part 450.

The bill requires the FAA to evaluate and report on the implementation of Part 450 and its impacts on the commercial spaceflight industry, including whether the rule has resulted in uncertainty or operational delays. The FAA must also continue an aerospace rulemaking committee comprised of launch and reentry service providers.

Further, the FAA must develop a digital system to accept commercial space launch and reentry applications and provide status information and notifications to applicants.

The bill elevates the Office of Commercial Space Transportation to a modal administration reporting directly to the Department of Transportation (DOT). The administration must exercise all of DOT’s authorities related to commercial space launch and reentry.

Finally, the bill revises the licensing process for private remote sensing systems and requires the Government Accountability Office to report on the Department of Commerce’s regulation of the private remote sensing industry. (Remote sensing generally refers to the collection of data by instruments in Earth’s orbit, such as satellites, that can be processed into imagery of Earth’s surface.)
How Does it or How Doesn't it Align?: Does not provide a framework for space sustainability, in-orbit tracking, or data sharing. Rather, its goal is to streamline launch, reentry, and remote sensing rules.
Sponsors/Original POCs: Sen. John Cornyn [R-TX], Sen. Ben Ray Luján [D-NM], Sen. Mark Kelly [D-AZ]

Legislation Name: Secure Space Act of 2025
Current Status: Referred to Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
Substantive Effect:
This bill prohibits the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) from granting satellite licenses or earth station authorizations, including U.S. market access for foreign-licensed satellites, to specified foreign entities of concern and their affiliates. (Earth stations, also commonly known as ground stations, are earth-based radio stations that communicate with satellites. A grant of U.S. market access permits one or more foreign-licensed satellites to communicate with one or more U.S.-licensed earth stations.)

Specifically, the FCC may not grant a satellite license, an earth station authorization, or market access to any entity, or an affiliate thereof, that produces or provides communications equipment or services deemed to pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States. (The FCC maintains a list of such equipment and services, known as the Covered List. Providers of such equipment and services include, for example, Huawei Technologies Company and ZTE Corporation.)
How Does it or How Doesn't it Align?: Does not provide a framework for space sustainability. Rather, prohibits the FCC from granting satelitte licenses or earth station authorizations.
Sponsors/Original POCs: Rep. Frank Pallone [D-NJ], Rep. Bob Latta [R-OH]

Legislation Name: Accessing Satellite Capabilities to Enable New Discoveries (ASCEND) Act
Issue: Commercial Satellite Data Acquisition; Orbital Safety
Current Status: Passed House; Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders
Substantive Effect:
This bill provides statutory authority for the Commercial SmallSat Data Acquisition (CSDA) program run by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA). Through the CSDA program, NASA acquires remote sensing data and imagery from commercial satellites to support its Earth science research. (Remote sensing generally refers to the collection of data by instruments in Earth’s orbit, such as satellites, that can be processed into imagery of Earth’s surface.)

Under the bill, NASA may establish or modify end-use agreements to allow for broad use of data and imagery acquired under the program, including by individuals outside of NASA (e.g., other federal agencies). The terms of any data or imagery acquisition may not prevent the publication of such data or imagery for scientific purposes or the publication of information derived from it. To the extent practicable, NASA must acquire such data and imagery from U.S. vendors.
How Does it or How Doesn't it Align?: Does not provide a framework for space sustainability. Rather, it focuses on NOAA weather/earth science research and forecasting and aims to expand commercial opportunities for providing weather data.
Sponsors/Original POCs: Rep. Brian Babin [R-TX], Sen. John Hickenlooper [D-CO]

Legislation Name: Space Modernization for the 21st Century
Substantive Effect: The Order overhauls the Commission's rules for licensing space and earth stations by replacing part 25 with a new rule part—part 100—that creates a "licensing assembly line" to process applications with greater speed and predictability. Part 100 allows an applicant to apply for a geostationary-orbit (GSO) system, a non-geostationary orbit (NGSO) system, a Variable Trajectory Space Station (VTSS) system, or a Multi-orbit Satellite System (MOSS). The GSO system application will now allow for multiple satellites operating together at a single orbital location in line with innovative new designs that industry is pursuing. The VTSS category will allow for requests that may not cleanly fit into the other categories, but represent a growing area of the space economy.
How Does it or How Doesn't it Align?: Aligns with Pillar 1: Modernizes domestic space licensing; requires all space station licensees and market access grantees to share ephemeris data, characterized by the FCC as a "meaningful step towards enhancing space safety"

Substantive Effect: Requests $11M for the Office of Space Commerce, funded through Commerce's Departmental Management account rather than NOAA. The congressional justification cuts 16 OSC positions and does not clearly fund continued TraCSS operations (reportedly about $1M to move the TraCSS pilot to a containerized format).
How Does it or How Doesn't it Align?: Conflicts with Pillar 1: The report calls for secure, sustained funding to fully operationalize a civil SSA/STC system like TraCSS as critical national infrastructure; this request would leave it largely unfunded for a second straight year.
Sponsors/Original POCs: Taylor Jordan (OSC Director)

Legislation Name: FY2027 Commerce, Justice, Science Appropriations Bill
Current Status: Approved by House Appropriations Committee; Senate committee action pending; government operating under a continuing resolution through 12/11/2026
Substantive Effect: Provides $50M for the Office of Space Commerce (within NOAA), well above the $11M requested, and directs continuation of TraCSS.
How Does it or How Doesn't it Align?: Aligns with Pillar 1: Restores funding for the civil SSA/STC backbone the report says Congress should fund securely and sustainably.
Sponsors/Original POCs: House Appropriations Committee Chairman Rep. Tom Cole [R-OK-4]

Legislation Name: Mitigation Methods for Launch Vehicle Upper Stages on the Creation of Orbital Debris (Withdrawal)
Substantive Effect: Withdraws FAA's 2023 proposed rule that would have required commercial launch providers to remove spent upper stages from orbit within 25 years of launch. FAA said it would further consider public comments, review its legal authority and industry cost inputs, and may propose orbital debris rules in the future.
How Does it or How Doesn't it Align?: Conflicts with Pillar 2: The report's life-cycle model depends on responsible end-of-life disposal and argues orbital carrying capacity cannot absorb defunct objects; the withdrawal leaves commercial upper stage disposal without a binding requirement.
Sponsors/Original POCs: Stephen Earle (OSC Space Policy and Outreach Branch Manager)

Legislation Name: FY2027 National Defense Authorization Act (House Commercial Space Domain Awareness Provisions)
Issue: Space Situational Awareness; Space Domain Awareness
Current Status: Approved by House Armed Services Committee; final passage not confirmed
Substantive Effect: House Armed Services Committee amendments would require the Space Force to develop a plan to ingest more commercial data into its High Accuracy Catalog and to brief Congress on transitioning commercial space domain awareness pilots into operational programs.
How Does it or How Doesn't it Align?: Aligns with Pillar 2: Supports the report's call for layered ground- and space-based sensing and a data fusion layer that merges government and commercial tracking data.
Sponsors/Original POCs: Rep. Jeff Crank (R-CO)
